newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU energy ministers make progress in gas talks.
newsitem.headline: EU energy ministers make progress in gas talks.

text.p: EU energy ministers made progress in talks on Tuesday on opening up natural gas markets to more competition but remained split on key issues and agreed that much work remained before a deal could be struck.
European Union Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis said he was optimistic a deal could be reached during the first half of 1997, calling Tuesday's session a "serious first step".
"I think we made progress today...I'm optimistic," he told a news conference, adding that there was the right political momentum for making further progress.
The ministers said they reaffirmed the need to complete the internal market in natural gas and that further work was needed to ensure a rapid conclusion under the Dutch EU presidency next spring.

It was the first ministerial debate on a compromise proposal from the Irish EU presidency designed to narrow the differences between countries pushing for fast and far-reaching liberalisation and those who are more sceptical.

The talks focused on central issues such as public service obligations, the unbundling of accounts, access of gas suppliers to national networks and how to handle long-term take-or-pay contracts, which dominate Europe's gas industry.
While ministers appeared to be in broad agreement on the first two issues, they remained far apart on access to the system and especially on the take-or-pay deals.
"There is a variety of opinions on the matter," said Emmet Stagg, minister of state at the Irish Department of Transport, Energy and Communications.
The differences of opinion partly reflect the fact that some member states, such as France, are big importers of gas while Britain and the Netherlands are major exporters.

The Irish proposal incorporates some elements from the EU agreement on electricity liberalisation which ministers reached last June after six years of wrangling, but diplomats stress that there are many differences between the two sectors.
For example, the EU imports a lot of natural gas from potentially unstable countries such as Algeria and Russia.
The market is also less developed, especially in countries such as Greece and Portugal which are only now setting up their gas markets and would need special safeguards.
In general terms, big producers such as Britain and the Netherlands are enthusiastic liberalisers while France and Belgium are seen as more cautious.
Unlike the agreement on electricity, which foresees a gradual and progressive opening up of national markets, the Irish presidency has proposed a one-off liberalisation for gas.
No figures on the level of market opening have yet been put forward and this looks certain to be a controversial issue.
Germany would like to see EU member states open up their markets completely from the beginning, a position which is not acceptable to several other member states..
On take-or-pay contracts, these may create problems in a liberalised environment as purchasers must buy gas at a set price regardless of whether they have a buyer themselves.
France, which imports 90 percent of the gas it uses, and other member states insist that this kind of contract must exist to ensure security of supply.
Under the presidency proposal on access to markets, member states may choose between two different systems; negotiated or regulated access.
